title: Commentary on 76.3
content: Mouquet and colleagues’ Viewpoint, “Too cute to be wild: what teddy bears reveal about our disconnection from nature” (https://doi.org/10.1093/biosci/biaf146), makes the strong case that pro-nature sentiments may be nourished from early stages of childhood development through cuddly toys that resemble wild animals. However, they also caution that “if the bear that comforts a child looks nothing like a real bear, the emotional bridge it builds may lead away from, rather than toward, true biodiversity.” I am continually drawn back to their ideas because they draw attention to, as they also note, so much research on how important properly functioning ecosystems are to the human psyche. If you want to get deeper perspectives on human health and prosperity, please keep an eye out for our forthcoming One Health Special Issue, headed by Mary Ann Ottinger. In another Viewpoint, “Restoring the Indus River Basin and its biodiversity” (https://doi.org/10.1093/biosci/biaf151), Shah and Wu “highlight the critical challenges faced by Pakistan’s portion of the Indus Basin, where human-driven stressors have increasingly jeopardized the basin’s natural ecosystem and biodiversity.” We emphasize that we welcome perspectives from the Global South, where so much of the world’s biodiversity is found. We have a thoroughly scholarly book review of Richard Hutto’s A Beautifully Burned Forest: Learning to Celebrate Severe Forest by a globally respected fire ecologist, Juli Pausas, in “In defense of severe fires” (https://doi.org/10.1093/biosci/biaf182). Pausas has been critical of simplistic and anthropocentric frameworks for describing complex natural processes. In his review, he states that “A Beautifully Burned Forest serves as an antidote to such simplifications and challenges the common belief that severe forest fires are inherently bad and provides provocative ideas that challenge current forest management practices.” One of our final Feature articles appears in this issue, “Illuminating Iridescence: Nature’s Shimmering Marriage of Geometry and Light” (https://doi.org/10.1093/biosci/biaf188), by Dybas. This is a beautifully written illumination of the subject by a noted professional science writer. The Features category was directed by Lesley Evans Ogden, a well-respected freelance science writer, so a big thank you to Lesley for your former service to BioScience. We hope that our new submission category, Notes from the Field, where we feature entertaining “short descriptions of natural history observations that have the potential to move our disciplines in terms of research, mentoring, teaching, outreach, and policy consequences” will serve as a substitute for the former Feature contributions.
